sections.b: Matthew follows Mark's words over the bread and cup and sharpens them: "Take it and eat"; "Every one of you, drink from it"; and, his own addition, the cup is "poured out for many, so that sins can be forgiven" (26:26–28). The meal is a Passover in Matthew, Mark and Luke, and its words echo the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) and the servant who bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Jesus vows not to drink the fruit of the vine until he drinks it new in the Father's kingdom (26:29). Matthew has no "do this in remembrance of me," but his church plainly kept the meal. The Where Christians differ cards at Matthew 26 set out how the churches read "This is my body" and "drink from it, all of you."

common: Most Christians through history have held that Christ is truly present in the Supper, though they explain the presence differently.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Supper was not a Passover meal at all, but a farewell meal the night before, as John's dating implies.

sections.b: Matthew dates Jesus' death by Passover (26:2) and makes the Last Supper a Passover meal (26:17–19), eaten reclining, with blessings over bread and wine and a closing hymn, probably the Hallel (26:30). The leaders fear a riot at the festival (26:5), and the governor's custom of releasing a prisoner belongs to it (27:15). John's Gospel places the crucifixion as the lambs were being killed; Paul calls Christ "our Passover lamb" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Matthew tells the crucifixion as an enthronement in mockery: the scarlet cloak, the crown of thorns, the reed, "Hail, King of the Jews" (27:27–31), the placard over his head (27:37), and two bandits at his right and left (27:38). Psalm 22 shapes the scene, from the dividing of clothes (27:35) to the taunt that God should get him free (27:43) and the cry "My God, my God" (27:46). Matthew adds signs no other Gospel has: an earthquake, split rocks and saints raised (27:51–53), and a confession by the whole guard (27:54).

common: Jesus' cry "My God, my God" quotes the first line of Psalm 22.
uncommon: Some scholars read the saints raised at Jesus' death (Matthew 27:52–53) as apocalyptic imagery rather than a reported event.

sections.b: Matthew's resurrection account has an earthquake, an angel who rolls back the stone and sits on it, guards who become "like corpses" (28:2–4), the women meeting Jesus and holding his feet (28:9), and a meeting with the eleven on a mountain in Galilee (28:16–20). Only Matthew tells of the guard at the tomb and the bribe to say the body was stolen, a story he says was still told "right up to today" (27:62–66; 28:11–15). The saints raised at Jesus' death (27:52–53) present his death and resurrection as the start of the general resurrection.

The risen Jesus tells the eleven to make disciples of all the nations, "baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them" (28:19–20). It is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus commands baptism, and the source of the formula used by nearly all churches. The order (make disciples, baptize, teach) is central to the debate over infant and believer's baptism, and the one "name" to the debate with Oneness Pentecostals; see the cards at Matthew 28.

Matthew's last chapters bring his relation to Israel to a crisis. "All the people" accept responsibility for Jesus' blood (27:25); the guards' story spreads "among Jews right up to today" (28:15); and the disciples, once sent only to Israel's lost sheep (10:5–6), are sent to "all the nations" (28:19). Readers differ on whether Matthew means that Israel is now replaced, or that the mission widens to include the nations alongside Israel. Most scholars today read 28:19 as including Jews, and read 27:25 as a judgment on one generation tied to the fall of Jerusalem, not on the Jewish people forever.

sections.h: The Son of Man before the high priest
sections.b: At his trial Jesus combines Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13: "from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the Power's right hand and coming on the clouds of the sky" (26:64). Matthew's "from now on" points to his vindication at the resurrection. The Gospel ends with the risen Jesus claiming "all authority, in heaven and on earth" (28:18), the words of Daniel 7:14.

Jesus is accused of saying he could destroy God's sanctuary and build it in three days (26:61), mocked with it on the cross (27:40), and at his death the sanctuary's curtain is torn from top to bottom (27:51). Judas throws his silver into the sanctuary (27:5). Readers see in the torn curtain open access to God (Hebrews 10:19–20), a sign of the Temple's coming end in AD 70, or both.

Jesus calls the cup "my blood of the covenant" poured out for forgiveness (26:28). Judas confesses "innocent blood" (27:4); the silver becomes "the price of blood" and buys the Field of Blood (27:6–8); Pilate declares himself clean of Jesus' blood, and the people answer, "His blood on us, and on our children!" (27:24–25). The repeated word draws on the law of innocent blood (Deuteronomy 21:1–9) and the formula of responsibility (2 Samuel 1:16).

sections.b: Only Matthew gives the price, thirty silver coins weighed out as in Zechariah 11:12 (26:15), Judas's question "Rabbi, it isn't me, is it?" (26:25), Jesus' "Friend, get on with what you came for" (26:50), and Judas's regret, confession of "innocent blood" and suicide (27:3–5). Matthew reads the purchase of the Potter's Field as fulfilling "Jeremiah" (27:9–10).

common: Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver.
uncommon: Some writers argue that Judas's regret in Matthew 27:3–4 was true repentance.

claude.title: Peter and Judas: where each one turns
claude.body: Reading Peter and Judas as a pair is old. John Chrysostom set Peter's tears against Judas' despair (Homilies on Matthew), and Davies and Allison note that Matthew puts Peter's tears (26:75) directly before Judas' regret (27:3). What I would add is a small point about who hears each man. Judas confesses, "I sinned" (27:4), to the chief priests, the only people in the story who cannot release him, and they answer, "That's for you to see to." Peter says nothing at all; he weeps, and the next word to him comes from the risen Jesus through the women, who call the disciples "my brothers" (28:10). On this reading, the contrast is less in the depth of their sorrow than in the person each one turns to. I have not seen this exact point made, but it builds on the traditional pairing above.

sections.b: Matthew alone has Pilate's wife send word about her dream and "that righteous man" (27:19), and Pilate wash his hands before the crowd, saying "I am clean of this man's blood" (27:24). Pilate appears again granting Joseph the body (27:58) and the chief priests a guard (27:65).

Matthew 28:19 is the only Gospel text that names Father, Son and Holy Spirit in one formula, "into the name" (singular) of all three. The Didache gives the same words for baptism around AD 100. All manuscripts have it; Eusebius's shorter quotations ("in my name") are generally judged paraphrases.

"His blood on us, and on our children!" was for centuries the chief proof text for the charge that the Jews killed Christ and were cursed for it. In Matthew it is a formula of responsibility spoken by a crowd the chief priests had persuaded; Matthew probably connected it with the destruction of Jerusalem a generation later (23:35–36). Some read a double meaning, since Jesus' blood is "poured out for many" (26:28). The Catholic Church (Nostra Aetate 4) and many other churches have rejected its use against Jews. See the deep dive at Matthew 27.

sections.h: His death and resurrection in Matthew
sections.b: Matthew presents Jesus as fully in command of his passion: he announces its date, names his betrayer, refuses the sword and the angels, answers the high priest under oath, and "let his spirit go" (26:2, 25, 52–53, 64; 27:50). He dies as "King of the Jews" and is confessed as "God's Son" by Gentile soldiers (27:37, 54). Raised by God, he receives all authority and promises to be with his followers every day, which answers his name Immanuel, "God with us" (1:23; 28:18–20).
